periods.activity_title: First Encounter — Read-Aloud and Choral Recitation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Recite (p.103): read aloud and choral-recite the poem.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud twice at a natural, expressive pace — once for pleasure, once with slight pauses at line-ends so students catch the rhythm. Students listen with books open on p.103.
Let us Recite (p.103): whole-class choral reading, stanza by stanza. Teacher models each stanza once; class echoes. Repeat until the cadence feels natural.
Students pair up and take turns reciting the poem to each other. Circulate, gently correcting pronunciation and rhythm.
Two or three volunteers recite independently. Brief whole-class appreciation: ask 'Which line did you enjoy saying most?' to close on a positive note.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's repeated phrase ‘Up in the air’ naturally anchors the swing’s back-and-forth rhythm — encourage students to sway gently as they chant it. Watch for students rushing the final ‘down’; a slight pause before it lands the punchline. No prior recitation preparation is needed; the choral echo structure builds confidence from scratch.

periods.activity_title: Think and Discuss — Personal Swing Experiences

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p.104): discuss personal swing experiences and imagined aerial views.

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick choral recitation of the poem (p.103) to settle the class and re-anchor the content. One stanza per row, whole class.

Let us Think B — Question 1 (p.104): ‘Have you seen a swing? Where? What was it made of?’ Students discuss in pairs, then pairs share with the class. Teacher lists different swing materials on the board (rope, wood, metal, tyre) as students mention them.

Let us Think B — Question 2 (p.104): ‘What would you like to see when you are up in the air on a swing?’ Students think silently for one minute, then share in a round-the-room format. Teacher notes imaginative responses (mountains, the sea, their house from above) on the board alongside the poet’s own list.

Bring the two discussions together: ask students to notice the overlap between what the poet actually saw (rivers, trees, cattle, countryside) and what they imagined. Close by rereading stanza 2 aloud together.

periods.teacher_notes: Having chanted the poem together, students are primed to connect Stevenson’s aerial imagery with their own mental pictures — the discussion flows naturally from the sensory details in stanza 2. Watch for students who conflate the poet’s view (a rural countryside) with an urban scene; gently note what the poem actually names without dismissing their ideas. Allow home-language responses and paraphrase in English to keep participation high.

periods.activity_title: Listening for Rhyme — Hear the Pattern, Add Your Own

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p.107): listen to the poem, list rhyming pairs, add two original rhyming words.

time_bands.activity: Briefly tell students they will listen especially for words that sound the same at their ends. Ask one student to give a quick example of a rhyming pair before the reading starts.

Let us Listen (p.107): teacher reads the poem aloud from p.103 three times at a steady pace. First read: students just listen. Second read: students jot or whisper rhymes they catch. Third read: students confirm their list.

Pairs compare their lists. Bring the class together and build a shared list on the board: swing–thing, blue–do, wall–all, wide–countryside, green–seen, brown–down. Discuss why the poet chose these end-words — do they feel satisfying or surprising?

Each student (or pair) adds two rhyming words of their own choice and shares aloud. Teacher records a few creative pairs on the board. Close with a final choral read of the poem, clapping lightly on the rhyming words.

periods.teacher_notes: Having discussed the poem’s imagery in the previous conversation, students are now listening with a sharper ear for sound pattern rather than meaning — this shift in attention is worth naming aloud at the start. The ABAB rhyme scheme means the rhyming pairs are two lines apart; some students may initially list adjacent lines, so a quick demonstration of ‘swing’ and ‘thing’ being four words and one line apart helps. Accept any phonologically valid pair students volunteer for the extension.

periods.activity_title: New Words and Comprehension — Reading the Poem Closely

tasks_in_class.task_brief: New Words (p.103–104): read and understand pleasantest, cattle, countryside.
Let us Think A (p.104): answer three comprehension questions about the poem.

time_bands.activity: Shared reading: teacher and class read the poem together from p.103, then teacher points to each New Word (p.103–104) — ‘pleasantest’, ‘cattle’, ‘countryside’ — in its line. Students say each word aloud and the teacher elicits or supplies a child-friendly meaning.

Let us Think A — Questions 1 and 2 (p.104): ‘What does the poet see when the swing goes over the wall?’ and ‘Does the poet enjoy swings? Which lines tell us that?’ Students locate evidence in the poem text, then share answers in a whole-class discussion. Teacher prompts with line references if needed.

Let us Think A — Question 3 (p.104): ‘Up in the air so blue — why do you think the poet says the air is blue?’ Students think quietly, then discuss with a neighbour before sharing with the class. Teacher accepts several interpretations and asks students to defend their view with a word or image from the poem.

Brief consolidation: teacher reads stanza 2 aloud slowly while students call out the sights the poet names (rivers, trees, cattle, countryside). Close by asking which of the three comprehension questions students found hardest and why.

periods.teacher_notes: Having listened to and recited the poem across multiple units, students are now shifting from sound to sense — they should be read to find specific evidence rather than just respond impressionistically. The word ‘cattle’ often puzzles urban children; a quick sketch or the word ‘cows and bulls’ on the board is enough. Question 3 is deliberately open-ended and links sky colour to childhood experience; welcome varied interpretations as long as students connect them to the poem.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn (p.104): practise sentence expansion by adding one detail at a time.

time_bands.activity: Write the seed sentence ‘The child swings’ on the board. Ask students what questions a reader might ask — ‘where?’, ‘when?’, ‘how?’ — and add one answer at a time, expanding it to three or four steps. Make the process visible and slow.

Let us Learn (p.104): read the textbook example (Jeevan waited → Jeevan waited for the bus → …) aloud together. Discuss what kind of detail is added at each step (place, time, reason). Students identify the expansion pattern with a partner.

Students frame their own expanding set of at least four sentences starting from a simple seed of their choice. Circulate and prompt those who are stuck by asking ‘what else can you tell me about when / where / why?’
Three or four volunteers read their expanding chains aloud. Class listens for the detail added at each step. End by asking: which sentence felt the most complete, and why?

periods.teacher_notes: The stringing-together exercise is a grammar-in-context task; students are not learning a rule in isolation but practising the writer’s craft of elaboration. A common pitfall is adding synonyms instead of new information (‘Jeevan waited and sat’) — model the difference between adding a word class and adding a fact. Praise expansion that uses concrete, sensory detail.

periods.activity_title: Words as Verb and Noun — Exploring Double-Role Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen — Verbs and Nouns (pp.105–106): circle verbs, underline nouns in five word-pair sentences.

time_bands.activity: Write ‘I swing on a swing’ on the board. Ask students what job each ‘swing’ is doing. Establish the idea that one word can be a verb (action) in one sentence and a noun (thing) in another. This sets up all five word pairs.

Let us Listen — Verbs and Nouns (p.105): work through ‘dance’ and ‘play’ as a class. Teacher reads each sentence pair; students circle the verb form and underline the noun form in their books. Discuss: how do you know which is which?

Students work in pairs on ‘answer’, ‘fly’, and ‘waves’ (p.106). Each pair writes a brief reason for each choice (‘fly is a noun here because it is the name of an insect’). Circulate and address confusion, especially with ‘waves’ where context determines the role.

Quick whole-class check: call out each word and ask a student to share the sentence where it is a noun and the sentence where it is a verb. End with a challenge: can anyone think of another word that works as both a verb and a noun?

periods.teacher_notes: Having practised sentence expansion in the stringing-together activity, students are now looking inside sentences at individual word roles — a natural progression from length to function. The word ‘waves’ is the trickiest because its noun form (ocean waves) and verb form (she waves) differ in both meaning and context; give it extra time. Encourage students to test role by substituting ‘the ___’ (noun marker) or ‘to ___’ (verb infinitive) if they are unsure.

periods.activity_title: The /W/ Sound — Tongue Twister and Phonics Drill

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak (p.107): tongue twister and /W/ phonics drill with word list.

time_bands.activity: Let us Speak (p.107): teacher demonstrates the ‘O’-shape lip position for the /W/ sound, then says the tongue twister slowly. Ask students to watch the lip shape. Whole class attempts the tongue twister once at a slow pace together.

Choral tongue-twister drill: class repeats the tongue twister four to five times, gradually increasing pace. Then small groups compete for the clearest pronunciation at full speed. Pause to correct any students producing a /V/ sound instead of /W/.

Word list drill (p.107): teacher says each word — fever, fewer, valley, white, vine, wise, win, wait, vet, wet — and students repeat. Then teacher sorts the words on the board: which words have the /W/ sound and which have a /V/ sound? Students come up and sort.

Pairs quiz each other: one partner says a word from the list, the other identifies whether it has /W/ or /V/ and produces the lip shape. A few pairs demonstrate to the class. Close with one final whole-class tongue-twister chant.

periods.teacher_notes: The /W/ vs /V/ distinction is a known difficulty for many Indian-English speakers; the physical prompt of making an ‘O’ lip shape is the most effective corrective tool and should be returned to whenever a slip occurs. The word list is deliberately mixed (fever and valley have /V/; white, wise, win, wait, wet have /W/) to build discrimination, not just repetition. Praise confident self-correction over accuracy at speed.

periods.activity_title: Writing About Free-Time Pleasures and Prepositions in a Garden

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write 1 (p.108): write a short paragraph about free-time activities you enjoy.
Let us Write 2 (p.109): fill in blanks with correct prepositions using the garden picture.

time_bands.activity: Let us Write 1 (p.108): teacher models planning on the board — writes ‘pleasantest things I do’ at the top, then jots three bullet points (drawing, playing cricket, reading) and shows how to convert them into two or three connected sentences. Students plan their own list silently.

Students draft their paragraph independently using their plan. Teacher circulates, prompting with ‘can you say why you enjoy it?’ or ‘can you give one detail about where or when?’ Peer response: read to a partner and ask if the paragraph is clear.

Let us Write 2 (p.109): teacher reads the task instruction and names the prepositions from the box: on, beside, between, above, in front of, behind, under. Students open the textbook to the garden picture and complete blanks 1–7 individually, checking each preposition against the visual.

Whole-class check of Let us Write 2: teacher calls out each blank number; a student provides the answer and points to the feature in the picture that confirms it. Any disagreements are resolved by returning to the picture. Both tasks are complete within this unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored the word ‘pleasantest’ during comprehension work on the poem, students now own it enough to use it as a springboard for their own writing. A common error in Let us Write 2 is confusing ‘between’ (two objects) with ‘among’ or ‘beside’; the garden picture is the deciding reference and should be kept open throughout. Both writing tasks close in this unit — students submit or share their paragraph before leaving.

periods.activity_title: Swings of Imagination — Draw, Write, and Explore

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p.110): draw a magical swing and write a short adventure paragraph.
Let us Explore (p.110): share known festivals or seasons linked to swinging on swings.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the unit: ‘Today we imagine. If a swing could take you anywhere — outer space, a jungle, inside a story — where would you go?’ Take three quick verbal responses to spark the room.

Let us Do (p.110): students draw their magical swing and destination (roughly five minutes for the sketch). Then they write a short paragraph — three to four sentences — about the adventure, including what they saw, heard, or felt. Teacher circulates with prompting questions.

Gallery walk: students place their drawings on desks and walk around to read two or three classmates’ adventures. They leave a one-word or one-phrase sticky note (or verbal comment) of appreciation. Reconvene.

Let us Explore (p.110): teacher asks ‘Which festivals in India involve swinging?’ Students share what they know — Teej, Janmashtami, Shravan month, Onam. Teacher briefly notes two or three on the board. End with a final whole-class recitation of the full poem from memory.

periods.teacher_notes: The drawing-then-writing sequence in Let us Do scaffolds imagination into language — students who are reluctant writers often find the sketch a generative prompt. Let us Explore draws on students’ cultural knowledge; accept any regional festival name and affirm its connection to the swinging tradition. The closing recitation from memory brings the chapter full circle through the poem that opened it.

items.item_stem: In the poem, when the swing goes over the wall, what does the poet see? Choose the correct answer.

options.label: A

options.label: C

options.label: D

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be drawing on personal imagination rather than the poem’s rural imagery.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the student may be guessing rather than locating the specific visual details in stanza 2.

expected_elements: Names a feeling (joy, freedom, excitement) from the poem.
Uses at least one detail (blue air, wide view, flying).
Connects the detail to why it feels pleasant.

expected_elements: Names two or more enjoyable free-time activities.
Uses a word expressing enjoyment (pleasantest, favourite, love).

items.source_context: Sentence expansion; dual verb-noun words (swing, dance, play, fly, waves); /W/ phonics drill.
items.item_stem: Read each sentence. Decide whether the highlighted word is being used as a noun (a thing) or a verb (an action). Choose the correct answer for each sentence.

options.text: In the sentence ‘A fly landed on the food’, the word ‘fly’ is a verb.
In the sentence ‘Can you answer the question?’, the word ‘answer’ is a verb.
In the sentence ‘The waves crashed on the rocks’, the word ‘waves’ is a verb.
In the sentence ‘We watched a play at school’, the word ‘play’ is a noun.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. True — ‘a play’ names a performance, so it is a noun. 2. False — ‘the waves’ names things in the ocean, so it is a noun. 3. True — ‘answer’ here means to do the act of answering, so it is a verb. 4. False — ‘a fly’ names an insect, so it is a noun.

items.source_lo: Student identifies word roles in context and produces the /W/ phoneme accurately using a poem’s vocabulary as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Sentence expansion; dual verb-noun words (swing, dance, play, fly, waves); /W/ phonics drill.
items.item_stem: Say these words aloud one by one: white, vine, win, vet, wait, wise, wet. Sort them into two groups — words where your lips make an ‘O’ shape for the /W/ sound, and words where your top teeth touch your bottom lip for the /V/ sound. Tell your teacher which group each word belongs to and why.

expected_elements: Correctly sorts /W/ words: white, win, wait, wise, wet.
Demonstrates visible lip shape difference for each group.

items.item_stem: Match each festival or month with the reason it is associated with swinging in India.
items.visual_stimulus:
Festival / Month | Why it is linked to swinging
Teej | Women swing and sing songs to welcome the monsoon
Janmashtami | Swings are decorated to celebrate the birth of Lord Krishna
Shravan month | Swings are set up in courtyards as part of seasonal celebrations
Onam | Swing games and folk activities are part of the harvest festival

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Teej – Women swing and sing songs to welcome the monsoon; Janmashtami – Swings are decorated to celebrate the birth of Lord Krishna; Shravan month – Swings are set up in courtyards as part of seasonal celebrations; Onam – Swing games and folk activities are part of the harvest festival.

answer_key.right: Women swing and sing songs to welcome the monsoon
Swings are decorated to celebrate the birth of Lord Krishna
Swings are set up in courtyards as part of seasonal celebrations
Swing games and folk activities are part of the harvest festival
